title: Batteries are hazardous waste
wrong: Mixed into ordinary waste, batteries crack and leak toxic metals and acid. They can also start fires.
right: Hazardous-waste collection keeps their metals and chemicals out of the soil and water.
principle: Hazardous waste needs its own collection route.
real_life: Drop used batteries at a collection point. Never put them in household trash.

title: Chemicals never go in the general bin
wrong: Leaking chemicals soak through the pile and into the ground, poisoning the water below.
right: Sealed and collected separately, the chemicals can be treated instead of spreading.
principle: Contamination travels: soil, then groundwater, then rivers.
real_life: Paints, solvents and cleaners belong at a household hazardous-waste site.

title: Plastic can be recovered
wrong: Thrown on the general pile, a perfectly good material is buried and lost for centuries.
right: Recovered plastic can be reshaped into new parts, like the housing for a water filter.
principle: Recovered materials replace the need for new ones.
real_life: Rinse and sort plastic for recycling so it can become something useful again.

title: Reuse starts with sorting
wrong: Usable metal buried under rubbish is gone for good, and so is the chance to repair anything.
right: Clean, sorted metal and pipe are exactly what a repair needs. Nothing new has to be made.
principle: Choose materials by what they are fit for, and reuse before you discard.
real_life: Repair and reuse first. Recycling keeps metals in circulation instead of in landfill.

title: Not everything can be recovered
wrong: Broken glass in the wrong bin injures whoever sorts it next and spoils the good materials around it.
right: Broken glass is inert but sharp. Bagged with general waste, it is safe for the people who handle it.
principle: Match each kind of waste to the right route, and not everything is hazardous.
real_life: Wrap broken glass before binning it. Local rules decide whether it is recycled.

title: Old electronics are hazardous and valuable
wrong: In the general pile, a phone leaks lead and cadmium, and its copper and gold are lost.
right: E-waste collection recovers the metals and keeps the toxins out of soil.
principle: Electronics are both a hazard and a mine of reusable metal.
real_life: Take old phones to an e-waste drop-off or a take-back scheme.

title: Some bulbs contain mercury
wrong: A cracked tube releases mercury vapour into the air you breathe.
right: Whole tubes go to hazardous collection, where the mercury is captured.
principle: Everyday items can hide hazardous contents.
real_life: Do not break old bulbs. Use a collection point that accepts them.

title: Food scraps are a resource
wrong: Food buried in a landfill rots without air and gives off methane.
right: Composted, the same scraps become soil.
principle: Organic waste is a resource when it stays out of landfill.
real_life: Compost at home or use your local food-waste collection.

title: Dry paper can be recycled
wrong: Soaked or soiled paper falls apart and cannot be reused.
right: Clean, dry cardboard goes back into the paper stream.
principle: Keeping recyclables clean keeps them recyclable.
real_life: Flatten cardboard and keep it dry until collection.

title: Glass recycles again and again
wrong: Glass in the general pile sits in the ground for thousands of years.
right: Recycled glass melts into new glass with no loss of quality.
principle: Some materials can be reused indefinitely.
real_life: Rinse glass and sort it by your local rules.

title: Cloth has a second life
wrong: Thrown away, textiles take up space and add to the pile.
right: Scraps become gloves, patches and padding.
principle: Reuse comes before recycling.
real_life: Repair, donate or repurpose clothes before binning them.

title: Metal can be recycled many times
wrong: Tin cans left in the pile rust away and are lost.
right: Recycled metal needs far less energy than making new metal.
principle: Recycling saves the energy already spent making a material.
real_life: Rinse cans and put them in the metal recycling stream.

title: Dirty recycling spoils the batch
wrong: Grease and food on cardboard can spoil a whole recycling batch.
right: Clean items recycle. Dirty parts go where food waste is accepted, or in the general bin.
principle: Clean sorting keeps recycling worth doing.
real_life: Rinse containers and tear clean paper from greasy parts.

title: Clear water is not always safe
wrong: You drink the clear sample. Clear water can still carry dissolved metals and chemicals.
right: The test strip shows what your eyes cannot see.
principle: Clear water is not necessarily safe water.
real_life: If water quality is uncertain, use a tested or treated source.

title: Each treatment stage does one job
wrong: A sand filter catches particles but does not remove dissolved chemicals.
right: A chain of stages, each matched to a problem, cleans the water step by step.
principle: Match each treatment stage to a contaminant.
real_life: Know what your water filter removes and what it does not.

title: Boiling is not a cure for everything
wrong: Boiling kills germs. It does not remove metals or chemicals.
right: Treat germs and chemicals with the methods that suit each.
principle: Match the treatment to the contaminant.
real_life: If chemical pollution is suspected, boiling is not enough.

title: Water carries pollution downhill
wrong: Rain washed the dump's leaking liquid into the river.
right: Sealed, sorted hazards cannot wash away.
principle: Where waste goes, water follows.
real_life: Keep chemicals, paint and oil out of drains and the ground.

title: Compost needs a balance
wrong: Only wet scraps turn to slime and smell. Only dry leaves barely break down.
right: A mix of dry material and wet scraps, kept damp, becomes soil.
principle: Balance makes soil.
real_life: Layer dry leaves or cardboard with kitchen scraps.

title: Plastic does not belong in compost
wrong: Plastic and metal do not rot. They stay in the soil as pollution.
right: Only organic material goes in the compost bin.
principle: Contamination ruins a whole batch.
real_life: Check your compost for plastic stickers and labels before adding it.

title: Soil is slow to build and quick to lose
wrong: Bare, lifeless soil blows away and washes out with the rain.
right: Covered, fed soil keeps its nutrients and its life.
principle: Soil takes centuries to build and moments to lose.
real_life: Keep soil covered with plants or mulch.

title: One system's waste feeds another
wrong: The food scraps you sorted at the dump would have rotted for nothing.
right: Here they became soil, and the soil grew food.
principle: Waste is a resource in the wrong place.
real_life: Close the loop: scraps to compost to food.

title: Labels tell you the danger
wrong: Guessing what a barrel holds can burn, poison or explode.
right: Reading the hazard symbol tells you how to handle it.
principle: Read the label before you touch it.
real_life: Learn the common hazard symbols and never open unlabelled containers.

title: Old equipment is full of useful parts
wrong: Scrapped as junk, a working solar panel is wasted.
right: Reused, it powers a whole system again.
principle: Old equipment is a store of useful parts.
real_life: Repair or donate working equipment before recycling it.

title: The cheapest energy is the energy you do not use
wrong: Wasteful devices overload a small grid and cause a blackout.
right: Efficient devices let the same power go much further.
principle: Efficiency makes renewable power stretch.
real_life: Switch off what you do not use and pick efficient appliances.

title: Batteries store power but become hazardous
wrong: A worn-out battery thrown away leaks again and spoils the soil.
right: Batteries store the sun's energy for the night, then go to hazardous collection.
principle: Treat storage as part of the whole system.
real_life: Return used batteries to a collection point.

title: Everything is connected
wrong: Each region tried to fix its own problem and pushed the cost onto the next.
right: Water, soil, energy and waste are one system: fix one and the others follow.
principle: Look for the loop, not the fix.
real_life: Ask where something comes from and where it goes before you buy it.

title: No one is coming
wrong: Everyone waited for someone else to act first: the council, the company, the neighbours.
right: Small actions by many people closed the loops the big plans never did.
principle: Responsibility shared is responsibility taken.
real_life: Start with what you can change at home, then help someone else start.
